opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my expectations have gone up quite a bit, but they've also become more nuanced.

A few years ago, when we started looking at egocentric data seriously, I thought of wearables as a nice supplement: a way to get some extra human demonstrations cheaply, while teleoperation stayed the real workhorse. The working assumption in the field was that the embodiment gap between a human hand and a robot gripper was simply too large, and that you'd always need robot-specific data to get anything working.

What changed my mind was seeing how much signal is actually in that human data once you capture it the right way. With devices like smart glasses you get head pose, eye gaze, hand tracking, and a first-person view that's surprisingly close to what a robot's head camera sees. When we co-trained policies on human and robot data together, we found that human data wasn't just filler. It actually improved generalization to new scenes and objects, sometimes more than adding the same amount of extra robot data would. That was a big shift for me.

The other thing is scale. Teleoperation is fundamentally bottlenecked by the number of robots and operators you have. Wearables flip that equation. If people are wearing these devices anyway, for productivity, for AR, for AI assistants, then data collection becomes a byproduct of everyday life. That's the only path I see toward internet-scale embodied data.

Where I've become more realistic is on the details. Passive, in-the-wild data is messy. People don't do tasks the way you'd want for training, and you're missing things like force and contact information that really matter for manipulation. So I don't think wearables replace robot data entirely. I see it more like a pyramid: a huge base of human wearable data that teaches the "what" and "where" of tasks, and a smaller, high-quality layer of robot data that grounds the "how" in the robot's own body.

So in short: I used to see wearables as a nice-to-have, and now I think they're likely a core pillar of how we'll scale robot learning. But there's a lot of research left in how to bridge that embodiment gap cleanly.

r001.rationale: The response says expectations have risen and describes wearables as a future path to internet-scale data, but it does not state that growing interest in human data accelerated Danfei Xu’s expected timeline for its availability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because I think my view has gone through a few phases on this.

A couple of years ago, when things like Aria glasses and Project Aria started becoming more accessible, I was honestly pretty optimistic. The pitch was very compelling: the bottleneck in robot learning is data, humans are doing manipulation tasks all day long, so if you can just put a camera on people and record everything, you get this enormous, diverse, in-the-wild dataset basically for free. No teleoperation setup, no robot in the loop, just people living their lives. And the ego-centric vision community had already shown you could collect at that scale, with Ego4D, Ego-Exo4D, and so on.

Where my expectation has shifted is less about whether the data is useful and more about what it's actually useful for. I used to think of it as something closer to a direct substitute for robot demonstrations, like you'd collect human video and then more or less retarget it onto the robot. In practice the embodiment gap turned out to be a lot more stubborn than I'd hoped. Human hands are not parallel-jaw grippers, humans don't move the way a seven-DoF arm moves, the viewpoint is different, and the contact information you really care about for manipulation is mostly invisible in a head-mounted camera. So the naive version of "train on human video, deploy on robot" has not panned out the way a lot of us imagined.

What I've become more convinced of is that wearable data is really valuable as a source of priors rather than as a source of policies. It teaches you a lot about what tasks look like, what objects are relevant, how a task decomposes over time, where people look before they reach, what the rough hand trajectory is. That's great for things like affordance learning, for learning task structure, for pretraining visual representations, and for giving a planner some notion of what sensible behavior looks like. But the last mile of actually closing the loop with the robot's own body still seems to need robot data, whether that's teleoperation or sim or real-world self-improvement.

The other thing that changed is that I underestimated how much the sensing side matters. Just RGB from glasses is pretty limited. The projects I find most exciting now are the ones that add hand tracking, sometimes gaze, sometimes even wearable tactile or force sensing, so the data is much closer to something a robot can actually consume. And interestingly, the hardware is converging a bit, because people are also building handheld grippers and exoskeleton-style devices that are sort of halfway between a wearable and a robot. That middle ground, where a human is still the one acting but the morphology and sensing are closer to the robot, is where I think a lot of the practical value is going to be.

So I'd summarize it as: I'm less bullish than I was on wearables as a drop-in replacement for robot data, and more bullish on them as one layer in a stack. The scale is real and the diversity is real. We just had to get more honest about what you can and cannot extract from it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes initial optimism and a later shift in how wearable data is useful, but does not say growing interest in human data accelerated Danfei Xu’s expected timeline for its availability for robot learning.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more optimistic about the scale of data we could get from wearables, but more cautious about what that data gives us directly. A wearable can capture what a person sees while cooking or cleaning, and that’s valuable for learning what people do, in what order, and in what context. But it doesn’t necessarily capture the forces they apply or all the details of how their hands interact with an object.

So I think of it as one part of the learning pipeline. Human video can help a robot learn what to do, while robot experience helps it learn how to execute that with its own body. The exciting possibility is that wearables could give us much more diverse examples of everyday activities. The challenge is turning those observations into something a robot can actually act on.

r001.rationale: The response says he has become more optimistic about the scale of wearable data, but does not state that growing interest accelerated his expected timeline for human data becoming available for robot learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more optimistic about the scale of data we could collect, but more cautious about how directly that data translates into robot skills. Wearables could give us a view of what people do in everyday life: what they pay attention to, how they approach a task, and how they recover when something goes wrong.

But seeing someone do something isn’t the same as knowing how to do it with a robot. You might see a hand picking up a cup, but you don’t necessarily know the force being applied or the contact conditions. And the robot has a different body.

So I see wearables as a potentially valuable source of context and behavioral examples. The question is how to connect those observations to robot experience, so that learning from human activity actually improves what the robot can do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he is more optimistic about the scale of wearable data, but does not state that growing interest accelerated his expected timeline for human data becoming available for robot learning.
